title: Postcard from the Moon
text:
Dear Grandpa,
Greetings from the moon! The flight here took {number} hours, and the pilot let me hold a {adjective} {noun} the whole time. The moon is very dusty and smells a little bit like {food}. My hotel room has a window, a tiny bed, and a big pile of {plural noun} in the corner.

Yesterday I went for a moon walk. Everything floats up here, so I {past tense verb} right over a crater by accident. A friendly moon guide named Doris showed me how to {verb} without bouncing away. She moves very {adverb} and wears a helmet shaped like a {noun}.

Tomorrow we get to visit the gift shop. I will bring you back a jar of {plural noun}. Please tell Mom I am still {verb ending in ing} every single night before bed.
Love,
Sam

title: Rules for the Space Station Kitchen
text:
Welcome to the kitchen on Space Station Ten! There is no gravity up here, so please follow these rules.

Rule one: Always buckle your sandwich to the table. Last week a sandwich got loose and floated right into Commander Lopez's {body part}. She was very {adjective} about it. Rule two: Do not open the jar of {plural noun} without asking. When it opens, everything inside drifts {adverb} around the room for a whole day.

Rule three: Drinks come in pouches. Please do not {verb} while you drink, or the juice will turn into {number} floating {plural noun}. Rule four: Pizza night is on Fridays. The cook makes it with tomato sauce, cheese, and a sprinkle of {plural noun}. Everyone eats it upside down while {verb ending in ing}.

If you see a {adjective} {noun} floating near the oven, do not touch it. Just shout "{exclamation}!" and the cleaning robot will come get it.

title: Help Wanted: Astronaut
text:
Help wanted! The Starlight Space Company is looking for a {adjective} astronaut to fly our newest rocket. The rocket is very shiny and is about the size of a {noun}.

Astronauts must be able to {verb} for three hours without stopping. You should also know how to steer with your {body part} and carry {number} {plural noun} at the same time.

On a normal day, you will check the engines, water the space plants, and say hello to the {plural noun} who live on the moon. Lunch is a tube of {food} and a {adjective} cookie.

To apply, please send us a letter and a drawing of yourself {verb ending in ing} in space. Our last astronaut {past tense verb} all the way to Mars and decided to stay, so we need someone new by Tuesday. Please write your letter {adverb} and in crayon.

title: Breaking News from Mars
text:
Good evening. This is Channel Seven News with a big story from Mars. This morning, a friendly alien named Zib opened the very first bakery on the red planet.

The bakery is small and {adjective}, with a sign shaped like a {noun}. The most popular treat is a muffin filled with {plural noun}. "I bake everything {adverb}," Zib told our reporter. "That is the secret."

The line was very long. Some customers waited {number} hours and passed the time {verb ending in ing} in the red dust. One astronaut was so happy that he {past tense verb} all the way back to his rocket.

Zib hopes to open a second bakery on the moon next year. For now, the bakery is open every day except Tuesday, when Zib likes to {verb} with friends. Now back to you, {name}, with the {adjective} weather report.

title: How to Make Moon Pancakes
text:
Moon pancakes are the favorite breakfast of every astronaut on the space station. Here is how to make them.

First, put two cups of flour and a handful of {plural noun} into a {adjective} bowl. Add one egg and a splash of milk. Stir it {adverb} with a {noun} until it looks like moon dust.

Next, pour the batter into a pan. There is no gravity, so the pancakes will float away, and you must {verb} to catch them. Flip each pancake {number} times. When it turns {color}, it is ready.

Finally, stack your pancakes on a plate and top them with syrup and {plural noun}. Commander Kim likes to eat hers while {verb ending in ing} past the window. Serve with a glass of {adjective} juice, and always say "{exclamation}!" before the first bite.

title: An Interview with the Moon
text:
Today our class newspaper got to interview the moon! The moon was very polite and only a little bit sleepy.

First, we asked what it does all day. "Mostly I float around Earth and look {adjective}," the moon said. "On weekends I like to {verb} with the stars." Then we asked about its favorite food. "Cheese, of course," it said. "But I also love a big bowl of {plural noun}."

Next, we asked who comes to visit. "Astronauts, sometimes," said the moon. "The last one brought me a {noun} as a present and {past tense verb} across my craters for an hour. It was very {adjective}."

Last, we asked for advice for kids. "Always eat your {food}," the moon said {adverb}. "Wear a {color} hat when it is chilly. And never stop {verb ending in ing} before bedtime." Then it waved goodbye and went back to work.

title: Captain's Log, Day Three
text:
Captain's log, day three. Our rocket is flying past Jupiter, and everything is going {adverb}. The crew had {plural noun} for breakfast again. Nobody complained.

At ten o'clock, a {adjective} comet zoomed past the window. It was shaped exactly like a {noun}. My copilot, a dog named Biscuit, {past tense verb} at it until it was gone. Biscuit is the best copilot in the whole galaxy, but he still does not know how to {verb}.

At lunch, the ship's computer said the engine was making a funny noise, like "{sound}." I fixed it with tape and two {plural noun}. Then I took a short nap.

Tomorrow we will land on a small planet covered in {plural noun}. I plan to spend the whole day {verb ending in ing}. I will bring my {adjective} flag and a snack for Biscuit.

title: How to Pack for Saturn
text:
Going to Saturn? Saturn is very far away, so you need to pack carefully. Here is what to bring.

First, pack a warm coat and {number} pairs of socks. Saturn is chilly, and the wind blows {adverb}. Next, bring a {adjective} helmet. The best helmets are round, clear, and about the size of a {noun}.

Do not forget your snacks. Most travelers bring crackers, apples, and a bag of {plural noun}. If you want to {verb} on Saturn's rings, you will also need roller skates and a {color} map.

Finally, pack something to do on the long ride. Many kids bring a book about {plural noun} or spend the trip {verb ending in ing} with their family. When you land, the Saturn welcome team will shake your {body part} and hand you a {adjective} snow cone.

title: Welcome Aboard Rocket Flight Nine
text:
Hello, passengers, and welcome aboard Rocket Flight Nine to the moon! This is your captain talking. Our trip will take about {number} hours. Please keep your seat belts on and your {plural noun} under your seat.

In a few minutes, a robot will come by with snacks. Today we have peanuts, orange slices, and warm {plural noun}. If you feel {adjective}, please press the blue light above your seat, and a helper will bring you a {noun}.

On the left side of the rocket, you can see Earth. It looks very small and {adjective} from up here. On the right side, you can see a family of space ducks {verb ending in ing} past the window. Please do not {verb} at them. They are shy.

We will land {adverb} on the moon at lunchtime. Thank you for flying with us, and have a {adjective} day.

title: Letter Home from Space Camp
text:
Dear Mom and Dad,
Space camp is going great! My bunk bed is shaped like a rocket, and my counselor, Ms. Rivera, is very {adjective}. Every morning we wake up at six and eat a bowl of {plural noun}.

On Monday we practiced floating in the big pool. I {past tense verb} so well that Ms. Rivera gave me a gold star. On Tuesday we built model rockets out of cardboard and {plural noun}. Mine flew {adverb} all the way over the {noun} before it landed.

Tonight we are having a star party. We will look through a giant telescope and try to {verb} the Big Dipper. My friend Max says he once saw a planet that looked exactly like a {food}.

Please send more socks and a {adjective} flashlight. I miss you and the {animal} very much.
Love,
Jordan
